headline: Demand for financial advice is massively outstripping supply of advisers in Australia, with AI emerging as a key part of the solution
reasoning: Colin Williams notes that there are roughly 240 entities per adviser based on Padua Solutions research, roughly double the current workload advisers can handle, indicating a significant structural supply gap. The shift toward micro-AFSL licensees (1-2 advisers) has increased compliance burdens on a per-adviser basis, making the economics harder. AI is already being deployed in licensed form to provide compliant financial advice under an AFSL, differentiating it from unlicensed tools like ChatGPT. AI is also being used to streamline compliance, file notes, and help clients prepare for adviser meetings, potentially increasing adviser capacity. Williams is watching US developments closely, including ChatGPT entering agreements to access bank accounts and investments to provide integrated advice.
quote: AI is definitely a big answer. And I mentioned that the number of entities that kind of translates around 240 entities per advisor, which is based on our research, is roughly double what we're currently doing now. So there's a big gap there. Huge gap. Um, AI, I think will play a part. And certainly from what we've seen today and we know it's changing rapidly, is playing a part where we currently have as recently launched was an AI business which is licensed and in other words, it can provide advice under an Australian Financial Services licence. So it's that there are some warranties, I guess you might say, with that advice, as opposed to something like a ChatGPT or a Claude or whatever, where you can get some advice, but it's not licensed.

headline: Australia remains significantly underserved by financial advice, with only around 40% of people over 60 forecast to seek advice despite most benefiting from it
reasoning: Williams is not optimistic that the advice gap will be fully closed, forecasting conservatively that only about 40% of Australians over 60 will seek financial advice, even though a case could be made that all of them should. Approximately two thirds of Australians reach retirement relying heavily on Centrelink for the majority of their income, meaning a large portion of the population is either unable to afford advice or does not perceive a need for it. While AI and structural reforms may improve access, the systemic nature of the gap means universal advice coverage is unlikely in the near term.
quote: I'm not as optimistic as in, everybody will get advice, like we were very conservative in that number of entities. For example, we forecast only around 40% of people over the age of 60 will want advice. Um, one could argue that everybody over 60 should be getting advice and we put 40%. But a lot of Australians will want to do it themselves. There's a lot of Australians who get to retirement. Roughly two thirds of the people get to retirement and rely heavily on Centrelink benefits for for a majority of the of their income stream as they retire. So not everyone is in a position to take advice or need advice, but I think it would be great to be in that position where everyone can get some advice.
